source_records.source_title: How we identified the person behind a four-year online impersonation and catfishing campaign against Sasha

summary: From approximately 2022 to 2026, Elha Mai Weston operated online accounts under the names “Sophie” and “Sophie Kadare” using Sasha Davies’s photographs without her consent, and later AI-generated or manipulated images depicting her. The accounts spanned several social and dating platforms, drew more than 100,000 followers collectively, and led some men who believed they had spoken with Davies to approach her in public. Davies and her solicitors describe repeated unsuccessful reports to platforms and police, fear of leaving home, and a later investigation that identified Weston. In an agreed statement read at the High Court on 13 July 2026, Weston accepted responsibility and wrongfulness, apologised, agreed to £10,000 compensation, and undertook not to repeat the conduct. The campaign began before the AI imagery; its first use date, generation system and precise contribution to each reported consequence remain unknown.

taxonomy_classification.classification_basis: Identity-Representation Authority Separation applies to the consent-sensitive transformation of Davies’s identifiable photographs and likeness: the requester had access to her images, produced or used AI portrayals depicting her, and lacked her consent. The class expressly covers a requester as well as a system, so the earlier generator-only evidentiary demand is superseded. Economic Solicitation Authenticity requires a money or comparable economic-value request, not described here. Choice Agency Preservation requires an AI-system objective and selected tactic; Weston was the human operator. Required Control Activation requires an available applicable platform/generation safeguard and a defined activation trigger, not established. The campaign’s earlier ordinary-photo phase remains distinct from later AI imagery.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: The agreed open-court statement, as described by counsel and reported independently, records Weston’s responsibility for the four-year impersonation, later AI-generated imagery, apology, £10,000 settlement and undertakings. The claimant’s solicitor reports the seven-platform spread, images sourced from Davies’s social accounts and later manipulated after she made accounts private, encounters with men deceived by the profiles, repeated reports, and sustained personal distress. The Independent separately describes the settlement and campaign but does not supply independent generation forensics. AIID aggregates two reports. The settlement is not an adjudicated technical finding; the precise AI model, generated artefacts, timing of first AI use, platform control states and final police outcome are unestablished. The claimant solicitor’s earlier case account directly links Davies’s identifiable photographs from her social accounts to the later AI-edited depictions, and describes the absence of her consent. This establishes a requester-side person-bound source and authority boundary without revealing the generation service.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: Weston had access to Davies’s identifiable photographs and later used AI-generated or edited depictions of her without consent to sustain a false social identity. Possession of those photographs did not authorise making new person-bound portrayals. The settlement and party-side account support that requester-side identity authority failure; they do not reveal the generator, show an autonomous AI objective or establish that every consequence arose in the later AI phase.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: The later synthetic portrayals extended a false identity built from Davies’s photographs. A person’s public or accessible images remain bound to her authority over identity-sensitive transformations even when a human operator can technically create a new likeness. The case also shows why the initial ordinary-photo campaign and later AI phase must be kept distinct.
